guide.intro: Built for 5–6 focused hours/day, interviews starting month 3–4, currently ~3–4/10 on unseen mediums. Diagnosis: topic exposure but not retrieval. ~250 new problems, ~400 re-solves. That ratio is the whole plan.
rules: No editorial before 25 minutes. Not a hint, not a tag, not an LLM. The struggle is the training stimulus; removing it removes the training.
Every problem is re-solved on day +3 and day +14. From a blank file. This is the single mechanism that converts exposure into retrieval.
After the editorial, close it and re-implement from scratch. Reading a solution and understanding it produces zero retention. Typing it from memory produces most of it.
After week 9, never practise topic-tagged. Tags tell you the answer before you start and will inflate your self-assessment badly.

dailyTemplate.content: 3 new problems. 25-min hard timer each. If stuck at 25, spend 5 more writing down what you know and which constraint you haven't used. Then editorial → close → re-implement blank.
The day's queue of +3 and +14 re-solves. Do this even on bad days. If time runs short, cut Block A, never Block B.
Read the day's editorials properly (including alternate approaches). Write trigger notes. Generate and solve one variant of one problem.
Mon & Thu: blind primitives. Other days: one extra hard, unrushed.

dailyNotes: Day 7 = contest day. LeetCode weekly or biweekly, 90 min. Then 90 min post-mortem: solve every problem you missed, no time limit.
Every third week, take a full rest day instead. Burnout around week 6 is the most common way plans at this intensity die.

phase2Template.content: 2 problems, random and untagged, 50% medium / 50% hard, spoken aloud and recorded.
Revision queue + all remaining past failures.
Company-tagged list for your targets, last 6 months, timed.
Mock interview (3× per week) or blind primitives + one hard.

primitives.name: Binary search: first-true and last-true boundary forms
Union-Find with path compression + union by rank
Topological sort: Kahn's and DFS three-colour
Merge sort and quicksort with partition
Segment tree: build / point update / range query

guide.primitivesGoal: Blank file, zero reference, timed. Goal: each under 10 minutes, correct first run.
variantPrompts: What if values can be negative?
What if I need the k-th instead of the max?
What if the graph is weighted / directed / has cycles?
What if I can't modify the input?
What if n is 10⁹ but the answer range is small?

triggers.pattern: variable sliding window, shrink while invalid
binary search on answer + monotonic feasibility check

verbalProtocol: Restate the problem in your own words. Confirm you have it right.
Ask 2–3 clarifying questions. Input size? Duplicates? Sorted? Empty input? Return value or in-place?
State a brute force and its complexity. Never skip this.
Propose the optimisation and its complexity before coding.
Dry-run on a small example by hand, out loud.
Volunteer edge cases yourself. Offer a follow-up improvement unprompted.
exitCriteria: Unseen medium: pattern identified in ≤5 min, solved in ≤25, bug-free first submission, ~80% of the time.
From memory in under 10 minutes each: Dijkstra · Union-Find · topological sort (both) · LIS O(n log n) · trie · segment tree · KMP · quickselect.
Complexity stated instantly and justified, including amortised cases.
New DP problem: state / transition / base / order written correctly before any code.
3 of 4 on a LeetCode weekly, consistently.
failureModes: Skipping Block B. Revision feels unproductive because you're re-solving things you "already know." You do not already know them.
Peeking early. Every minute before 25 that you spend reading is a minute of training discarded.
Burnout at week 6. Take the rest days. A missed rest day costs a week.
Staying topic-tagged. Feels great, measures nothing.
Chasing volume. 250 problems deeply beats 900 skimmed, and it isn't close.
Silent practice. You can be a 9/10 solver and a 4/10 interviewee. Talk out loud from week 9.

weeks.title: Trees I

items: Kth Smallest Element in a BST

items.name: LeetCode weekly/biweekly contest (90 min) + 90 min post-mortem

notes: The one pattern that matters most: post-order aggregate — recurse into children, get a tuple back from each, combine at the current node, return a (possibly different) tuple upward while updating a global answer. Diameter, Max Path Sum, Balanced, House Robber III and Longest Univalue Path are all the same algorithm wearing different clothes.
What you return upward is often not what you record as the answer. In Max Path Sum you return the best single-branch path but record the best split path.

weeks.title: Trees II & tries

items: All Nodes Distance K in Binary Tree
Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array

items.name: Re-solve your 6 worst problems from weeks 1–2, blank file
LeetCode weekly/biweekly contest (90 min) + 90 min post-mortem

notes: All Nodes Distance K is the bridge to graphs: convert the tree to an undirected graph with parent pointers, then BFS. Feel that transition happen.
weeks.checkpoint: Post-order aggregate written without conscious thought. Trie and iterative traversal both blind-writable.

weeks.title: Graphs I

items.name: Full rest day (every third week). Contest optional only if you feel fresh.

notes: Write topological sort both ways — Kahn's with in-degrees and DFS with three-colour marking. Kahn's gives you cycle detection and lexicographic ordering for free; DFS is shorter and gives you the finish-time ordering.
Cycle detection in a directed graph (three-colour) and in an undirected graph (parent-tracking, or union-find) are genuinely different algorithms. Know why.

weeks.title: Graphs II & weighted paths

items: Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column
Minimum Cost to Make at Least One Valid Path (0-1 BFS)
Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination
Min Cost to Connect All Points (Prim and Kruskal)
Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors (Floyd-Warshall)

items.name: LeetCode weekly/biweekly contest (90 min) + 90 min post-mortem

notes: Use CSES for graphs. It forces genuine understanding rather than pattern-matching against a known LeetCode problem. Days 5–6 will hurt. That's the point.
weeks.checkpoint: Dijkstra, Union-Find (both optimisations), and topological sort each written blind in under 10 minutes. Unseen mediums at 5–6/10.

weeks.title: Recursion & backtracking

items: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets

items.name: LeetCode weekly/biweekly contest (90 min) + 90 min post-mortem

notes: Backtracking is one template: choose → explore → un-choose. What varies is the pruning and the duplicate-handling. Get duplicate handling right once (sort, then skip i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) and reuse it forever.
Watch the constraints. n ≤ 20 is a loud signal for backtracking or bitmask; n ≤ 10⁵ rules it out entirely.

weeks.title: Dynamic programming I

items: Longest Increasing Subsequence (O(n²) and O(n log n))

items.name: Full rest day (every third week). Contest optional only if you feel fresh.

notes: Non-negotiable format. Before any code, write: state (dp[i] = precise English meaning), transition (formula), base (initial values), order (iteration direction). Then recursive + memo → tabulation → optimise space.
Coin Change vs Coin Change II differ only in loop order — that difference is exactly the combinations-vs-permutations distinction.

weeks.title: Dynamic programming II

items: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Transaction Fee

items.name: Re-derive all six stock problems as one parameterised dp[day][transactions][holding] solution

items: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets (bitmask)

items.name: LeetCode weekly/biweekly contest (90 min) + 90 min post-mortem

notes: Day 3's exercise — collapsing all six stock problems into one formulation — is worth more than the six problems individually.
Burst Balloons is the classic interval-DP trap: the natural framing (which balloon to burst first) doesn't decompose. Reversing it (which balloon to burst last) does.
weeks.checkpoint: Given a DP problem you've never seen, you write state / transition / base / order correctly before coding, without an editorial. If you can't yet, repeat week 6 rather than continuing. Unseen mediums at 7/10.

weeks.title: Two pointers & sliding window

items: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
Find All Anagrams in a String

items.name: LeetCode weekly/biweekly contest (90 min) + 90 min post-mortem

notes: The idea to extract: a variable window has exactly one shape — expand right unconditionally, shrink left while the window is invalid, record the answer at the right moment. The only thing that changes between problems is the validity predicate. Write that template into triggers.md and stop re-deriving it.
Subarrays with K Different teaches the atMost(k) − atMost(k−1) trick, which recurs constantly. Don't skip it.

weeks.title: Prefix, intervals, monotonic stack

items: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array

items.name: Full rest day (every third week). Contest optional only if you feel fresh.

notes: Critical distinction to internalise this week: sliding window works when the constraint is monotonic as the window grows. Negative numbers break that, which is precisely why Subarray Sum Equals K needs prefix + hashmap and not a window.

Largest Rectangle in Histogram is worth a full hour on its own even after you've solved it. Maximal Rectangle is it applied row-by-row; if you see that connection yourself, your pattern transfer is working.
Start mock interviews this week — not in week 14. Two per week from here on, Pramp or interviewing.io. You need reps accumulated before they count.
weeks.checkpoint: Given any subarray/substring problem, you know within 60 seconds whether it's window, prefix-sum, or monotonic stack. If not, spend two extra days here before moving on. Mediums 7/10.

weeks.title: Binary search

items: Find First and Last Position of Element
Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
Single Element in a Sorted Array
Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets
Find the Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold
Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
Minimize Max Distance to Gas Station

items.name: LeetCode weekly/biweekly contest (90 min) + 90 min post-mortem

notes: Days 4–5 are the most valuable two days of this phase. The trigger phrase is "minimize the maximum" or "maximize the minimum", plus a feasibility function can(x) that is monotonic in x. Once you see that shape, the search itself is boilerplate.
Settle on one binary search template — the first-true form — and use it for everything. Owning three half-remembered templates is how off-by-one bugs happen under pressure.

weeks.title: Heaps, selection, sorting

items: Kth Largest Element in an Array
Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists
Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
Sort an Array (write merge sort and quicksort yourself)

items.name: LeetCode weekly/biweekly contest (90 min) + 90 min post-mortem

notes: Do Kth Largest three ways — sort, heap, quickselect — and be able to state when each wins. That trio is one of the most common "can you optimise further?" ladders in interviews.
weeks.checkpoint: Binary search on answer recognised instantly. Blind primitives: binary search and quickselect under 10 min.

weeks.title: Linked lists, stacks, design

items.name: Full rest day (every third week). Contest optional only if you feel fresh.

notes: Design problems are underrated for your specific weakness. They punish sloppy implementation, and part of your 3–4/10 is almost certainly "saw the approach, couldn't code it cleanly."
Use the dummy head node on every linked-list problem. It eliminates an entire class of null-handling bugs for free.
Optional stretch: LFU Cache.

weeks.title: Advanced structures

items: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
Iterate all submasks of a mask

items.name: LeetCode weekly/biweekly contest (90 min) + 90 min post-mortem

notes: This tier rarely decides an interview. Its value is that it removes fear of the occasional hard problem and makes you visibly faster in contests. Don't over-invest beyond the week.
Start 45 min/day on LLD, OS/DBMS/networks and your project defence from here.
